en: The *Jñānasiddhi* composed by the illustrious Indrabhūti. First Chapter.
Homage to Vajrasattva!
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, who is worshipped by all the supreme Victors, who consists of all Buddhas, who pervades all accomplishments, and who is like the sky; (1)
I shall, with devotion and with my whole being, describe that supreme sādhana of the Omniscient One, the Excellent Vajra-holder, who bestows everything upon all sentient beings. (2)
Those fools who do not know the unsurpassed Vajrayāna, as taught in all the Yoga Tantras, wander here in this ocean of existence.
But those beings who have ascended [to this path], free from all conceptual constructions—those practitioners touch supreme enlightenment right here in this very life. || 4 ||
Those who are intent upon mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth, as well as recitation and meditation,
do not attain supreme accomplishment even in tens of millions of incalculable eons.
One should not harbor pride in one's mind regarding the perfection of physical form and youth, nor wealth, power, and strength, nor that which pertains to one's birth and lineage. (6)
One should not harbor the thought in one's mind: "I am wise," "I am learned," "I am skilled in all arts and crafts," or "I am a king. (7)
Though he be virtuous, learned, heroic, and even endowed with beauty and other such qualities,
he does not perceive a self, either in his own liberation or in the liberation of others.
"Vajrasattva himself abides, pervading the minds of all sentient beings"—having reflected thus, the yogi whose self is yoga should not conceptualize anything at all. (9)
One should not show contempt for those who are childish, foolish, poor, immoral, or afflicted by disease, nor for others endowed with many such [conditions]. 10.
Devoted to the Three Jewels, faithful, adorned with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), compassionate toward all sentient beings, and established in the vows of the samaya. || 11 ||
The knower of reality should always consume dried meat and blood mixed with the bodhicitta, combined with a great quantity of water. 12.
For the sake of attaining the ultimate reality (tattva), one who is free from all conceptual constructions should consume human flesh, horse, meat, cow, lamp-oil, elephant, and donkey. 13.
One should cause the destruction of the arising of the three realms of existence, seize the wealth of others, lust after the wives of others, and utter false speech. || 14 ||
By that very karma through which beings are cooked in a terrible hell for even hundreds of millions of eons, by that same [karma] the yogin is liberated. 15.
The yogin, endowed with great skillful means and acting for the benefit of the world, has no forbidden act that is loathsome to all sentient beings. 16.
(2) "Through the union of wisdom and skillful means, no evil is proclaimed.
Thus spoke the Vajra-holder himself, the manifestation of Vajrasattva. 17.

Free from the distinction between what may and may not be eaten, avoiding what may and may not be drunk, and liberated from the distinction between who may and may not be approached, the concentrated yogi shall become such. 18.
One should investigate all things as existing through dependent origination—devoid of coming and going, unarisen, and without self. (19)
One who understands [the truth] applies the analogies such as "like an illusion" and so forth; the knower of the reality of yoga should not form the conceptual constructions of "I" and "mine. (20)
The great vajra is all-pervading, established in all space;
it pervades the minds of all sentient beings and is the source of the great arising of all merit. || 21 ||
The Vajra is the mutual pervader, the all-knowing leader of the world;
this King Vajradhara is extolled in all mantras. || 22 ||
He who possesses the grace of the Guru shall attain the supreme reality;
otherwise, the fool, deluded for a long time, suffers in vain. (23)
The Guru is the Buddha, the Dharma, and indeed the Saṅgha as well;
through his grace, that supreme Triple Gem is known. (24)
For those blinded by the darkness of ignorance, he is the guide who reveals the path;
he shall be the foremost of all happiness and the bestower of all desires. (25)

One whose self is established in the profound ultimate of the Dharma, whose nature is solitude and compassion, who seeks to establish the Three Jewels, is free from worldly motives in the gift of Dharma. || 26 ||
(3) "That guru who correctly accepts disciples and emulates all the Buddhas—of him the Lord of the World has spoken; indeed, no others are known as gurus. (27)
Since there is no one equal to that great sage worthy of worship, therefore the practitioner should worship the excellent guru with every effort. (28)
There exists no person in the world equal to him, nor anyone in the three realms worthy of such honor;
Vajrasattva himself abides in the world for the sake of all prosperity. (29)
He is to be propitiated in manifold ways by disciples desiring the wealth of the virtuous,
and by those whose merit is undiminished and who seek to overcome all obstacles and impediments.
For this is the unsurpassed commitment (*samaya*) of all commitments;
it must be constantly guarded by you, as it bestows all prosperity. || 31 ||
Having obtained the supreme, divine knowledge that is free from all conceptual constructions, one who is indeed consecrated by the vajra-knowledge shall accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment. 32.
If one who is not endowed with right knowledge should receive initiation upon a mandala made of drawings or clay, he will indeed fall from his spiritual attainment.
From the violation of the samaya, there will be physical and mental suffering;
his wealth shall be destroyed, and death will come very quickly. (34)
And having experienced the suffering of hell for even hundreds of millions of eons after death, one might eventually emerge [only] to be born into a low-born family such as that of a Caṇḍāla. (35)
That foolish person is born either mute or deformed.
For he will be born blind in every birth, birth after birth; of this there is no doubt. || 36 ||
The wisdom of all the Tathāgatas is known as the Vajrayāna; one who is consecrated by that is called "the wise one, the consecrated. (37)
That yogi, who is the self of all Buddhas, is to be saluted by the hosts of all gods with palms joined in reverence; he is the Lord of the World. (38)
The heroic Bodhisattvas of great power provide protection;
and the Buddhas, the Great-Souled Ones with vajra-bodies, remain ever present. (39)
For he is devoted to truth and righteousness, a promoter of the Buddha’s path; those endowed with spiritual power praise him with reverence. (40)
Likewise, the world-protectors and others of great strength and prowess remain stationed, protecting him wherever he may be.
And whatever obstacles of Māra are established throughout all the worlds, they too do not create obstacles for him; terrified, they depart. (42)
All the gods and other perfected beings, including all that moves and is stationary in space—
even they, fearing the states of woe, do not transgress him.
Even for one who has attained the perfection of knowledge and discernment through diligence, ruin occurs if, out of the power of delusion, they transgress while being utterly bewildered. (44)
The omniscient one, the giver of boons, the speaker, who is devoid of color and shape;
liberated from coming and going, he is unshakable by any winds.
(5) It is not burned by a mass of fire, nor is it submerged by water;
indeed, it cannot be pierced even by a sharp weapon, despite great effort. 46.
Non-abiding like space, all-pervasive, and devoid of characteristics—this is that supreme reality, the unsurpassed vajra-wisdom. 47.
It is renowned as Samantabhadrā and designated as Mahāmudrā;
this should be known as the Dharmakāya and also as the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśajñāna). (48)
Just as one's own reflection is certainly seen in a mirror, so too the Dharmakāya is seen within the wisdom that abides like a mirror. (49)
The knowledge of all Tathāgatas and that of oneself and of living beings are said to be the knowledge of equality when they are realized as having a single nature. (50)
Primordially pure, unarisen, and luminous by its very nature;
it is known as the discerning wisdom because it is the non-dual, all-pervading knowledge. (51)
The performance of all Buddha-activities everywhere and at all times is called the accomplishment of duties, because it constitutes the single unified activity of all Buddhas. (52)
When everything obscured by the afflictions and the knowable has been liberated, then it is known as "perfectly pure" by the Vajrins, the supreme yogins. (53)

Likewise, because it is the singular enjoyment of all Buddhas with respect to the dharmas for those to be trained and the entire multitude of desired objects, the body is considered to be the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya). || 54 ||
Endowed with all the marks, yet indeed bodiless and without characteristics;
because it is an emanation of the Buddhas, the body is considered the nirmāṇakāya. || 55 ||
Having understood that through its true nature, the yogi, free from all conceptual constructions, attains accomplishment in this very life for the sake of the realization of Mahāmudrā. (56)
It should be known as Mahāmudrā, consisting of all Buddhas and auspicious;
it has been accomplished and taught by the excellent yogi in numerous tantras. (57)
One should measure the womb-wheel (garbhacakra) at every moment in each field;
there, the practitioner should properly maintain the state of all the Tathāgatas. 58.
All his childhood play, as well as the display of his various arts, his departure from the inner apartments, and likewise the subduing of Māra; || 59 ||
The descent from heaven, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the great parinirvāṇa, and whatever other playful manifestations there may be—[he displays them all]. (60)
The yogin should constantly visualize everything as consisting of all vajras;
for nothing new is seen by him, nor is there anything previously established that is not to be joined [with reality]. 61.
One should behold everything— every activity of all the Tathāgatas, every auspicious thing composed of vajra, and whatever exists throughout the three times— as being entirely so.
The yogi should contemplate such a state, which transcends the domain of all speech and is devoid of all characteristics, for it bestows the state of all Buddhas. || 63 ||
Meditating upon the perfected state— which is liberated from all stages and devoid of cause and effect—
the yogi attains accomplishment in this very life.
For the yogin who knows all methods and rituals, the supreme Vajradhara,
the unsurpassed reality is accomplished, just as in the case of the excellent Vajrasattva.
Whether standing, sleeping, sitting, or even walking about, and while speaking or uttering vajra-words, one should maintain the state of Vajrasattva. (66)
Always observing the vow, one should undertake the practice with the thought: "Having enjoyed forms, sounds, tastes, and touches, I perform worship to all the Buddhas. (67)
At that time, one should likewise give food, clothing, and so forth to sentient beings, or whatever else there may be; in this same manner, one should carry out the ritual procedure.
One should worship the Supreme Self with dances, songs, and instrumental music, as well as with flowers, garlands, and ornaments, with flower-wreaths, chowries, and umbrellas.
The yogi, recollecting all the Buddhas, should worship himself according to the ritual, even when anointed with fragrant perfumes, ointments, and the like. (70)
Whether he be an observer of vows, a shaven-headed ascetic, a householder, or a servant; whether a king, a minister, or a superintendent—let him act as a vow-holder according to his own inclination.
In that same way, this yogi acts; he is not defiled in any way, being liberated from all conceptual constructions and performing actions according to his will. (72)
He is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, the all-pervading one composed of all Buddhas; he is self-arisen, moves at will, and dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings. (73)
The yogi of reality should meditate while recollecting all reality;
having become accomplished as consisting of all vajras, he shall swiftly attain the state of Vajra. 74.
In this state, there are no obstacles nor any Māras; all things become subject to one's will.
The practitioner, observing the vow, should realize the self as completely liberated from all suffering. (75)
(8) Buddhahood in its entirety is accomplished in a single day even if devoid of ritual procedures, for the one of great vows who always perceives himself as united with all [deities]. 76.
One should always worship oneself with all the various kinds of offerings;
likewise, one should give them to others while recollecting Vajrasattva. (77)
Having gathered all living beings produced from food, as well as those born from excrement, the great yogi should consume them for the sake of attaining reality.
At the time of the ritual, one should always consume the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) together with great lamps and other things that are loathed by others; likewise, the Tathāgatas are to be worshipped.
One should not show contempt for a woman, even if she is despised in all her limbs; one should worship a woman born of any family as the bearer of the Vajra. 80.

Abiding in the practice of non-conceptual ritual, one should serve her who is endowed with flowers that have not yet bloomed and possessed of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), for the sake of attaining the reality (*tattva*). 81.
By serving a woman born of a Caṇḍāla family, or especially a Ḍombī, or one born of a despised lineage, one shall attain accomplishment. 82.
A yogi may desire maidens born of the families of the twice-born;
however, he should act in such a beautiful manner that his mind does not become corrupted. 83.
One whose nature is Vajrasattva should worship with beds mixed with coverings and mingled with excrement and the like, with a mind free from conceptual construction. (84)
Acting according to one's desire and performing whatever actions one pleases, one shall accomplish the state of Vajrasattva; otherwise, one will certainly suffer. 85.
(9) One does not achieve success through practices such as vows, fasts, and observances, nor through the meditative cultivation of the forms of deities endowed with various arms. 86.
Buddhahood is not attained even by those of great heroism through the recitation and visualization of mantras for kalpas as numerous as the atoms of Jambudvīpa. (87)
By means of these and many other doctrines devised by children, how could birth in a happy realm be difficult to obtain, and how could one become Vajrasattva? (88)
The Blessed One, the Sage, taught the great maṇḍalas, mudrās, and so forth, for those whose selves were free from the capacity for the union of perfect gnosis. (89)
Those who are unable to grasp that unsurpassed jewel of reality, which is by nature self-cognizable, through the investigations of logic and scripture; || 90 ||
Enveloped by the delusion of ignorance and possessing unexamining intellects, those beginners who grasp [only the literal] are vessels for the inferior dharma. || 91 ||
They were answered by the Lords of the World through the meditations on Vajrasattva, as well as by means of mudrās and maṇḍalas endowed with [specific] arms and colors. 92.
Those who, through other means, are vessels for profound wisdom, are unshakable by evil friends and by the obstacles and hindrances of Māra. || 93 ||
This pure reality of theirs is free from all conceptual constructions; it is inaccessible in every way to all sentient beings, including Brahmā and the others. (94)
This most wonderful and supreme gnosis, which bestows accomplishment even in this very life, which consists of all Buddhas and is auspicious, has been taught by the Lords of the World. (95)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Exposition of Reality, in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
(10) The second chapter:
Because they have the nature of the five Buddhas, the five aggregates are remembered as the Victors (*jina*).
The elements are Locanā and the others; therefore, they are considered to be the Buddha-body. || 1 ||

If all living beings were thus always already perfectly awakened within the three realms, then all practices for the sake of awakening, including hearing and meditation, would be entirely in vain. (2)
Because he is the Buddhahood of the entire world, it is not logical that he should be afflicted by the thirst for pleasure and pain, or by other such sufferings, within the three realms of existence.
Furthermore, the six supernormal knowledges and other such qualities and powers for enlightenment—how could these not manifest if there were a Buddha-body? (4)
How could one who does not understand in this way become a perfectly awakened Buddha? If anyone understands in this way, that person will become a Buddha. (5)
That yogi in whom contemplation proceeds through the gradual application of practice shall become a Buddha; others are not achievers of Buddhahood.

If those Buddhas [arise] from intrinsic nature, they have no need for cultivation through practice; therefore, cultivate that which is consistent with reason, which is always endowed with logic and free from what is illogical. (7)
If some person who is destitute of protection should imagine, "I am the king," he would not obtain the kingdom even in a hundred million eons.
Since his kingdom does not exist due to false conceptualization, therefore Buddhahood will not arise due to false cultivation. || 9 ||
(11) In the King of Tantras, reality is indicated by names associated with the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth, expressed through conventional terminology. 10.
Semen is known as Vairocana, and likewise, it is the imperishable Vajrodaka;
the female organ is like a lotus, and the male organ is like a vajra. (11)
The body of the deity does not arise from an intrinsic nature; therefore, it is not logical to speak of it as such.
Since it cannot be spoken of in accordance with either reasoning or scripture, [it is beyond conceptualization]. || 12 ||
If Vajrasattva were to be a created form of a deity, then he would be conditioned; consequently, he would perish like a jar or similar objects. (13)
Consequently, the practice of awakening would become fruitless in its many forms;
furthermore, for what purpose would there be cultivation if, having arisen, it were to perish? (14)
How is form created by the mind said to be conditioned?
And how does it perish? Listen now to this from the ocean of delusion. 15.
This is indeed a conceptual construction of the mind, and it too possesses the characteristics of the conditioned. How could that which is constructed by the mind be indestructible? (16)
Now, I shall meditate upon that divine form, endowed with the colors of the arms and established exactly as it was previously positioned, though it has not yet been physically fashioned.
If that uncreated form of the deity is being meditated upon by you, what is the purpose of meditating on something that was previously established and yet remains unproduced? (18)
"I shall become such a form"—this is the meditation based on the thought "I am.
In this practice for accomplishing the form, the yogi should investigate these two types of meditation. (19)
(12) If one forms the meditative visualization, "May I become like that," then when that meditation has become clear, she is seen as the deity. 20.
When meditation is practiced after having observed the form on a cloth or similar object, then for you who have [thus] arisen, O wise ones... || 21 ||
If that unborn form of the deity has entered into that meditative absorption,
then by virtue of the engagement of all superknowledges, that very form [arises] at that very moment.
If that is so, then what you have attained through meditation is not correct.
Do you not realize that the form produced by you is something created? 23.
But if one holds the position that "I am that," then duality does not exist there;
since there is no proof for what is already established, how can there be the conceptualization of meditation? (24)
For the Omniscient One does not desire to attain omniscience again;
rather, you must perform the work of a Buddha, for Buddhahood is not brought about by another. (25)
Thus, since you lack correctness, how can you conceive of falsity?
That the work of a Buddha remains unaccomplished is itself my own vain conceit.
The uncreated nature of the deity’s form is now being examined.
It cannot be said to be uncreated, because it possesses form, like a jar or similar objects. (27)
For this very reason, the Lords of the World, in order to awaken the ignorant, demonstrate nirvāṇa itself as a means of showing the impermanence of form. (28)
Therefore, the Buddha, being devoid of intrinsic form, does not appear anywhere in the world;
for the sake of establishing the form of the Buddha, one should not practice the meditation on form. (29)
(13) Buddhas are not material according to logic; for how could one who is non-material and possesses the six superknowledges be a material entity localized in a specific place? || 30 ||
In world-systems, within the bases of form and so forth such as the body and so on—there is no arrival of those [objects] into the bases of the eye and so forth. (31)
When the movement of the eyes and other [senses] is not perceived at all, how can there be their conjunction? Since they lack such connection, there can be no omniscient being.
If he were to go there and know it, how could he possibly be capable of knowing it gradually?
Even so, he would not be omniscient, because the objects of knowledge are infinite in their true existence. (33)
Therefore, the Buddhas have no need for eyes and the other sense organs;
nor is any body found that is distinct from the eyes and the rest. (34)
For the Buddha-body is indeed obtained as motionless as a statue;
because of the absence of conscious experience, the form of the Buddha is not omniscient. (35)
The Buddhas, who are compassionate, are recognized as possessing the divine eye;
since they possess all [faculties] such as the divine ear, how could they not be omniscient? (36)
If one were to know by means of cognition, then what would be the use of the Buddha-body?
That cognition knows what resides within the body; therefore, the body itself is indeed all-knowing. (37)
Will the Buddha-knowledge be distinct from the body or non-distinct?
If it were conjoined with the body, it would surely perish in nirvāṇa. (38)
Because the body is subject to destruction, knowledge also perishes;
therefore, it is not logical that the Buddhas possess a vow consisting of both knowledge and body. (39)
(14) If knowledge were to reside in the body, then in the absence of the body, there would be no omniscient one;
since knowledge arises dependently, it would therefore meet with destruction.
Omniscience is not tenable for those whose bodies of cognition are subject to destruction;
for this reason as well, the Buddha-body is not established as being omniscient. (41)

But if it were a position that [the Buddha-body] is other than gnosis, how could there be a body of the Buddha? For it would be more appropriate for a yogin to say, "It is merely an image of the Buddha. (42)
Therefore, the world that wishes to meditate upon form is more deluded than even the most foolish; it is like one who wishes to eat space for the sake of accomplishing the wisdom of a Buddha.
Those who lack compassion for sentient beings and are devoid of faith and wisdom will have no understanding of the profound and vast teachings. 44.
While these people, devoid of Dharma and deluded by it, run here and there like madmen, they all proceed simultaneously toward their downfall.
Great compassion must be exercised even toward those who are inferior to sentient beings;
therefore, it is not appropriate for those who teach right knowledge to treat others with contempt. (46)
The second chapter: The Refutation of the Cultivation of Form in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
(15) The third chapter:
Vajrasattva is not realized through the cultivation of form.
Likewise, even conceptualization involving mental images will not accomplish Vajrasattva. || 1 ||
That cognition is either just the form itself, or it is [the cognition] set aside from the form.
If the form were the cognition, then this much would not be tenable. (2)
If it does not possess the form [of the object], then that is not cognition, for cognition does not lack the nature of having a form;
just as space cannot be a jar, nor can a jar be space. (3)
Form would not exist without the formless; indeed, one who is formless does not possess form.
Knowledge is declared to be formless, while forms are remembered as belonging to that which possesses form.
How indeed could there be oneness between those two? The conceptualization that the form is nothing but cognition is not at all tenable. (5)
Moreover, because it would entail other faults, listen now in brief:
if cognition indeed has the form [of the object], then it follows that it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). (6)
An unconditioned entity does not exist in the world;
because it is produced, how could there be perishability in the wisdom of a Buddha? (7)
The Tathāgata declared it to be peaceful, without beginning or end;
and his illustrious sons spoke of it as unconditioned knowledge.
For all that which appears is declared to be like an illusion;
since there is neither arising nor ceasing, how could it be knowledge? (9)

(16) If that which is the path of visual consciousness were conceptualized by means of knowledge, it would follow that the Buddha-knowledge is subject to change; otherwise, this would not be the case.
That knowledge of all Buddhas is shown to be unchanging;
therefore, it is certain that it is not logical to speak of its being one. (11)
This appearance belongs to cognition; that [external object] is not postulated as cognition. Since the appearance has ceased, why would cognition not also cease? (12)
Therefore, oneness is unestablished, as is quite certain by your own words;
for what purpose indeed do you postulate oneness [in vain]? (13)
Because it contradicts both reasoning and scripture, and because it is entirely fruitless, it is not at all tenable to claim that knowledge possesses a form. (14)
If cognition were distinct from its form, cognition would not be tenable;
cognition occurs when there is an object of cognition, but not when the object of cognition is disregarded. (15)
If it is conceived that cognition is distinct from the forms, then the forms must likewise be distinct from cognition, which would be without a basis. (16)
At the time of the arising of cognition, however, there is no emergence of forms;
if forms were to arise, cognition itself would not be possible. (17)
Just as when a jar is produced, the arising of a cloth does not occur, so too is it observed in the world that phenomena are distinct from one another. (18)
(17) For one cannot become the possessor of a son by means of a son who has not been born; likewise, how can cognition that lacks a support be held to possess an aspect? 19.
In relation to what could cognition be "with form," such that it would become so?
It is simply called "cognition with form" [in relation to its own appearance], but it is not [a cognition] devoid of form. (20)
How could there be the possession of an aspect in a cognition that is devoid of aspects?
That which is accompanied by aspects is conceived as "having an aspect" (sākāra). || 21 ||
How could the wisdom of a Buddha be free from all aspects?
If, even without an aspect (ākāra), there were to be "possessing-aspect" (sākāratva) here, then how could the Buddha be reality without the Buddha-knowledge? || 22 ||

That would not be knowledge, nor would there be an omniscient one, if [reality] were conceptualized through separate cognitions; furthermore, if knowledge possessed a mental image (*sākāratā*), its establishment as valid cognition would never be possible. (23)
If it were to possess the state of having an aspect (sākāratva) merely by being joined with an aspect,
it would not be observed as being endowed with conjunction, like the Buddha who sets [the world] in motion.
For there can be no conjunction whatsoever between that which possesses form and that which is formless;
just as, due to its conjunction with space, the arising of a jar would not occur. (25)
If having an aspect were to be established by virtue of being endowed with an aspect, then, because of its dependence, it would follow that it is perishable and subject to the worst adversity. (26)
That which arises dependently cannot be the wisdom of a Buddha;
for if wisdom were conditioned, its being endowed with mental aspects would not be established. (27)
(18) And if there were indeed a difference between the form and the cognition, how could that which is distinct from one another be called "cognition," as I have stated?
If it is conceived that the aspects arise from a distinct cognition, then it follows that they would be non-cognition because they are other than cognition. (29)
Just as [an object] other than the forms [of cognition] would be formless, why is it not likewise conceived that cognition is formless? (30)
In the *Jñānasiddhi*, the third chapter is the refutation of [the theory of] cognition with form.
(19) The fourth chapter:
But that which was proposed according to reasoning has been refuted as having form.
It cannot be formless; this is what is now being explained.
Even if cognition were formless, it would still be conceptual;
since it is devoid of forms, how could such a thing be all-knowing? (2)
He would not possess omniscience, nor would there be the designation "knowledge" for him;
furthermore, insentience would follow for one who does not perceive all aspects. (3)
That which is non-inert and of the nature of consciousness is traditionally known as formless;
how could that which knows everything truly know what is unreal?
One who knows all phenomena to be devoid of self and free from all conceptual constructions—how could such a person perceive that knowledge as false? (5)
Having awakened to all phenomena through such analogies as being like an illusion,
it was taught in various places by all the Buddhas for the benefit of the world.
But those examples such as illusion and the like, which are conceived through false conceptualization, do not exist by way of their own nature; how then can he who knows them be omniscient? (7)
One does not perceive a rabbit's horn, nor likewise the son of a barren woman;
because they are non-existent, how could one perceive them? Therefore, [the object] must be formless.
For the arising of illusion has been pointed out as the illustrative examples by the Victors together with their sons.
Non-existence as mere conceptual construction is not established in any way whatsoever. || 9 ||
(20) If those properties are considered to be in every respect equal to the examples,
then they would not be examples at all, because [the property to be proved] would itself be that which is yet to be proven, despite all effort.
The analogy of the lion applied to a person proceeds in the world based on the possession of qualities such as valor, and not because of the presence of a tail and other such physical features. (11)
Therefore, all things do not exist as non-existent in every respect by way of their own nature;
this should be understood by the best of men in accordance with both reasoning and scripture. (12)
Therefore, that which has been pointed out by you, following the path of deceiving the ignorant, is not what those intent on uplifting the world declare to be reality. (13)
Just as the horn of a hare is a non-entity, and like the son of a barren woman, so too have the Victors never taught that there is an absolute non-existence of all entities anywhere. (14)
If entities such as form and so forth do not exist at all in any way whatsoever, how is the divine eye of the Buddhas, whose nature is compassion, established? (15)
Consequently, the divine ear and all other such [superknowledges] would not exist;
for, in the absence of these superknowledges (abhijñās), one could not be omniscient. || 16 ||
When the Buddha-body is perfectly joined with formless cognition, all superknowledges proceed; how then could omniscience not exist? 17.
These bases of form and so forth are experienced by the eye and the other [senses] alone, together with the mind; thus does it proceed in the world. (18)
"You yourself have stated again and again that form and the other aggregates do not exist;
how then can it be conceived that there could be a union with non-existence? (19)
(21) If there were a connection with non-existence, such a thing as you have said might be appropriate;
but for those for whom there is non-existence in every respect, how can a connection with that be desired?
Likewise, even in the absence of formal yoga, knowledge arises through the power of aspiration;
it accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings according to the capacity of those to be trained. 21.
When he does not know anything at all, how can he act for the benefit of sentient beings?
For one who lacks knowledge is not omniscient, and there is no compassion in the gathering of sentient beings.
Because he accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings through his vow like another wish-fulfilling gem, it does not appear to the wise here that this is due to devotion toward him. (23)
Because it is always certain in the complete accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings, that non-inert gnosis is known as the wish-fulfilling jewel. (24)
Where even regarding the unseen, one’s own conceptualization of knowledge arises—why indeed could it not occur that "I am omniscient" and "I have become the lord of the world"? (25)
Having generated the thought of awakening and being equipped with all the accumulations, one should possess great enthusiasm and great heroism through meditation, reflection, and so forth. (26)
Through such things as hearing the true Dharma, there is no longer any need for suffering;
there is no arising of what was previously non-existent, and that which was previously established perishes. (27)
If such is Buddhahood, then everything [else] is entirely in vain;
for [the Buddha] is liberated from fears such as death and from the torments of hell. (28)
Free from the sufferings of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and so forth, and being non-inert by nature, one who knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is indeed called "omniscient. (29)
(22) "He who possesses knowledge of intrinsic nature is omniscient," so it was taught by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Because he knows everything through direct perception, he is called "Omniscient."
It destroys the hellish suffering that causes one to wander in saṃsāra, and one obtains the happiness of a universal monarch and the like; of this there is no doubt. || 31 ||
The Fourth Chapter: The Refutation of the Formless [Cognition] in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
(23) The Fifth Chapter: If it is argued that [the formless theory] is not [tenable] because it is thus confused by faults; then—
Therefore, the reality of mindlessness is now being refuted. (1)
Those deluded ones desire a knowledge that remains in a state of extreme ignorance; through their deluded disposition, those of wicked conduct surely attain only further delusion. (2)
In this world, it is logical that the fruit should be similar to its cause;
for rice never arises from *kodrava* grain. (3)
Therefore, non-conceptual knowledge is not established as being [inherently] so;
otherwise, the non-conceptuality of knowledge would not be tenable. (4)
The Tathāgatas have declared that non-conceptuality is the true nature of knowledge;
however, for one who is ignorant of reality, the mere conceptualization of non-conceptuality [is not true knowledge]. (5)
Therefore, the Buddha-knowledge is known to be effortless and non-conceptual;
yet, due to the presence of intentional compassion, it does not become a state of mindlessness.
The state of non-conceptuality is not taught anywhere as ignorance;
for there is no higher dharma than this for those who perceive reality otherwise.
The omniscient and all-seeing one, the benefactor of all the world, has been taught in various places by the Lords of the World, whose very nature is compassion. (8)
(24) If it is argued that there is only non-conceptual recollection, then why are all these words not likewise recollected? 9.
Because it is devoid of both objects [of knowledge and the knower], there is neither knowledge nor an omniscient one;
this reality has been refuted, for such is the false knowledge of the deluded. (10)
The fifth chapter: The Refutation of Deluded Conceptions regarding the Accomplishment of Gnosis.
(25) The sixth chapter:
Neither inhalation nor exhalation can be the reality.
Even if it were to exist between those two, how could it be the element of air?
Since there is nothing at all in the middle, how can it be the reality?
If the wind were the reality, it would be on the side of the bellows.
Just as one might blow air into a bellows for the purpose of fanning it, so too does the body blow upon the mind for the sake of its projection. (3)
There is no one who blows with the breath, nor likewise one who is blown by the breath, just as there is no one who blows the body, like a smith blowing a bellows.
No distinction is seen between those two by the yogis who perceive reality:
in respect to the activity of burning and splitting, they are equal to fire and the mind.
The wind of inhalation and exhalation is equal to the air from a bellows;
just as the air in a bellows is in its true nature, so too is the wind within the body.

When the bodily wind has emerged through all the gates as the reality (tattva), it is not appropriate to call it "reality," because the wind is characterized by its state of pervasion (āveśa). || 7 ||
For those who have fallen from the path, who are deluded, and who proclaim false truths, there is no birth in a happy realm; their only destiny is hell.
The sixth [chapter], the Refutation of Consolation in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
(26) The seventh chapter:
Some base men say that the mouth produced by the two organs is the reality (*tattva*).
The supreme Victors do not at all proclaim that reality is great bliss. || 1 ||
That which arises through dependent origination is not reality anywhere;
for that [reality] does not exist at any time by way of its own intrinsic nature.
The gnosis of all Tathāgatas has the nature of self-cognition;
because it is the supreme state of all bliss, it is known as "Great Bliss" (mahāsukha). || 3 ||
Impermanent great bliss is not at all the eternally permanent great bliss;
how could that which arises from scratching an itch be great bliss? Indeed, it is not.
There is no pleasure equal to passion; bestowing that upon the Victors, one may enjoy all sensual desires and should never feel any sense of disgust.
In all the *Yogabhadra* [tantras], it was taught by Vajrasattva for the sake of the mental happiness of yogins; it is not the reality from the perspective of the ultimate truth.
The seventh chapter: The Refutation of the Counterfeit of Great Bliss in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
The eighth chapter:
Since self-cognition has been refuted, there is therefore no such thing as correct cognition.
All principles are false and imagined by those who are deeply deluded.
Other [erroneous views] as well should be refuted by the wise through their own intelligence;
now, that true reality (tattva) by which it may be correctly attained is being proclaimed. (2)
Sentient beings of limited intellect, possessing little merit and little vigor—how may they attain the supreme knowledge of all the Tathāgatas? (3)
I shall now declare the sequence taught by all the Buddhas:
having placed his knees firmly upon the ground, he stands well-established.
Then, full of faith, with body upright and palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus:
"The Perfectly Awakened Ones who will appear in the world in the future shall likewise [uphold] the teaching. (5)
I pay homage to all these Buddhas, the revealers of the true Dharma, both those present and those who have passed away—those who point out the ultimate reality. (6)
I offer myself for the service of worship;
may the Leaders accept me as belonging to all the Buddhas. (7)
And worshipping the Teachers of the World with all the various supreme offerings, extending as far as the realm of space and encompassing Mount Sumeru; || 8 ||
By all the various excellent offerings produced from the dharmadhātu, and by all the miraculous manifestations of Vajrasattva belonging to the past and the future; || 9 ||
(28) Having confessed all evils that have arisen, the knower of reality should again undertake the vow of non-action. 10.
Whatever merit belongs to all the Buddhas and their wise sons, to the community of Śrāvakas and the Buddhas, and whatever other merit belongs to all embodied beings; || 11 ||
With a joyful heart, I rejoice in all the merit that has been performed throughout all births, whether it be my own or that of others.

Mounted upon the chariot of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatattva), abiding everywhere in the ten directions, skilled in illuminating the Dharma and possessing minds of great compassion—may you reveal the teachings; I now offer this petition. (13)
With palms joined in reverence, he asked: "When and how shall all living beings become Buddhas and remain established in that state? (14)
Let those Protectors who act for the benefit of all sentient beings remain for now;
[let us consider] whatever merit has been performed or caused to be performed by body, speech, and mind. (15)
And whatever has been rejoiced in, by that may the world become all-knowing;
having worshipped with flowers and other offerings according to one's ability throughout the three periods of the day. (16)
Having prepared a mandala for all the Buddhas and for the Vajrasattvas, one should arrange the five nectars, either mixed together or unmixed. (17)

One whose self is liberated from all conceptual constructions should undertake the pledges and so forth—the commitment-restraint established in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-tantra* and other such scriptures. (18)
One should not kill living beings, nor should one take what is not given;
one should not engage in sexual misconduct, nor indeed should one speak falsehoods. (19)
(29) One should avoid drinking intoxicants, for they are the root of all misfortune;
as well as slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. 20.
I shall generate in every way ignorance, hostility toward sentient beings, and false views that have never arisen before; yet I shall establish them in nirvana.
Then one should take up all the branches of meditative concentration and the supreme vow;
likewise, one should generate the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), which brings about the great arising of all merit. (22)
Having established all beings, even the great ones, upon the stages of omniscience, may I, whose nature is compassion, become the remover of all their suffering. (23)
The giver of all prosperity and the instructor of the path to enlightenment, one should correctly generate the mind [of awakening] toward the equality of all living beings. (24)
This should be known as the thought of awakening; otherwise, it would be false.
That which remains in a state of imbalance is not truly called the thought of awakening. (25)
That gnosis which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end does not arise;
all the Vajradharas never perform any empowerment.
Even all the gods and others do not protect him from his enemies;
therefore, the yogi who knows the means is the sole kinsman of all sentient beings. (27)
Having generated a firm mind that is non-deceptive, by this act the Perfect Buddhas, who are the embodiment of all that is done, become pleased. (28)
Those possessed of great strength and prowess perform an empowerment;
neither Māras, obstacles, nor calamities, nor those seeking an opportunity for entry can prevail. (29)
Vajrapāṇi and the others, being delighted, provide constant protection;
and that best of men attains purification from all sins. (30)
(30) Furthermore, from the arising of all merit, the arising of right knowledge occurs; otherwise, the arising of the principles of reality would not occur in any way whatsoever. (31)
Therefore, one who knows the ritual procedure and desires to attain that knowledge for the sake of accomplishment and freedom from affliction in this very life should act at the outset. (32)
For the sake of destroying all obstacles and increasing longevity and health, this must necessarily be performed by a yogin who desires its fruit. (33)
Taught with compassion by the Buddha-vajrin in various tantras:
this yogin established on the path becomes like the moon in the bright fortnight;
he undergoes a process of increase and never experiences decline. (34)
When someone of inferior vigor does not attain Buddhahood, they may instead exercise the sovereignty and happiness of a universal monarch throughout all their births. (35)
The supreme Victors declare that whatever merit belongs to all the Buddhas existing in all directions and times, it resides upon the tip of a single pore of his skin. (36)
In the *Jñānasiddhi*, this is the eighth chapter: the means for attaining the equipment of merit and knowledge.
Chapter Nine:
(31) How can even most terrible evil be brought to exhaustion through teaching?
And likewise, how is merit fully enjoyed through sympathetic rejoicing? (1)
In some tantras it is said that acts such as causing death through lethal weapons must be performed, while in others it is said they must not; how is this not a contradiction? (2)
Likewise, everything such as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) is understood to be inedible;
how then can there be the arising of auspiciousness through those many things that are unpleasant and so forth? (3)

I shall explain these in their proper order, as they have been demonstrated in various tantras by all the Buddhas [along with the Vajra-holders], for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect. (4)

Whatever action is performed through body, speech, and mind—there is no fourth [agent] other than these; thus it is investigated. Furthermore, without the mind, the body would not be capable of performing anything at all.
And without that [cause], the word could never exist at all.
Therefore, bodily and vocal actions belong to you, while that which is mental is non-dual;
for it is by the mind alone that the entire world is created, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Whatever action results in the welfare of others is entirely a virtuous deed;
the Supreme Victors declare that its opposite is non-meritorious. (8)
(32) "Indeed, by the mind alone all that which is auspicious and inauspicious is performed; by the mind alone comes destruction. Thus spoke the Teacher of the World. 9.
Whatever evil is proclaimed to be accomplished through harming sentient beings, one should generate a mind of benefit and confess that which has been transgressed. (10)
Whatever harmful act was previously committed with zeal, its destruction occurs through its very opposite, for it is by that same means that it was produced.
Just as someone who has fashioned a jar might break it himself,
so too he who has produced evil may destroy it by his own self.
If a fool thinks, "I shall teach later," his teaching is not appropriate, nor does his sin perish. (13)
Likewise, the destruction of merit occurs in exactly the same way;
even when merit has been performed, there is no doubt that it will come to ruin due to the presence of flaws. (14)
And when, while giving, the desire to give does not exist in the mind, then even though it has been given, that merit will not accrue to anyone. (15)
It is the supreme place for all, wherein everything perishes—even the great merit accumulated over thousands of millions of eons. (16)
The accumulation of the equipment of merit by one who has generated the thought of awakening, though acquired over hundreds of millions of eons, perishes in a single instant. (17)
In such a case, there is no other second [duty] more important than protecting one's younger brother who is disliked; for that reason, it has been thus declared by the Tathāgatas. (18)
In that ocean of virtues, because it is the source of all happiness for everyone, even a very small benefit would result in a great mass of merit. (19)
(33) Some extremely deluded fools, who do not perceive either reasoning or scripture, say that sin arises from mere conceptual construction; such are those who destroy themselves. || 20 ||
If a yogi free from conceptual construction is not defiled by sins, then it is not logical for him to undergo transformation when there is a cause for the arising of hatred and the like. (21)
Otherwise, if one were to abandon worldly conduct, would anything not become possible?
For instance, would it not then be as reasonable to travel on one's head or to subsist by eating stones? (22)
For him, affliction by cold, wind, thirst, and the like is not possible;
nor should he experience distress from harms such as verbal abuse. (23)
If one's own duty—which is difficult to abandon when drawn by greed and other passions—is performed without conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), it would not be so in any other case. (24)
In this world, there is no non-arising or destruction of evil deeds;
moreover, due to the association with anger and egoism, evil is not purified.
It is postulated that the deity alone performs all of that; yet why would this deity not cause it to be done much more intensely even prior to its production? (26)
"This is a false conceptualization, that a deity alone performs [the action]; for this activity belongs to those who are overcome by greed and desire to act. (27)
The wise, who possess the wealth of intelligence, should understand that all mental efforts here, such as rejoicing and so forth, are endowed with the accumulation of merit. (28)
May that inferior merit, which is accompanied by body and speech, be equal to the merit praised by the Buddha for one whose mind is exclusively and intensely focused. (29)
(34) Any action such as the harming of living beings performed by one whose mind is possessed by greed and the like will not be wholesome; all merit, however, arises from compassion.
Whatever action is performed for the sake of others' welfare by those whose very nature is compassion, all that they who fulfill the hopes of the world call "merit. (31)
Even that which is forbidden is permitted out of compassion for those of firm resolve, but not for those whose bodies are devoid of mercy and who are overwhelmed by self-interest. (32)
Even when merit has been performed, for one who hates a person, it results in nothing but evil; so the supreme Jinas declare.
And it has been said: "Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, for Bodhisattvas everything becomes auspicious until the end of the eon, because their minds are under their own control. (34)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Instruction on the Thorough Knowledge of the Arising and Destruction of Sin and Merit, in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
(35) The Tenth Chapter: For the sake of removing obstacles, those intent on the perfecting of the mind [should consume] the five nectars;
likewise, even the flesh of goats and other animals has been prescribed for yogins by the Victors.
All living beings, even while consuming everything, are not awakened;
those fools do not understand, their thoughts devoid of wisdom.
Since it is composed entirely of impure elements, the body is indeed not pure;
if someone were to consume its secretions, would not everything that has been eaten be consumed by him? (3)
Likewise, for all embodied beings, whether they are known as eaters of what is fit to be eaten or what is unfit to be eaten, purity is never established in anything such as milk and the like.
One realizes that all foodstuffs are impure,
because their origin here is seen to be from water.
Having washed away all that is foul with a mass of rainwater and having brought all the crops to fruition, it then enters the ocean and other such bodies of water.
The water raised by the nāgas, who are joined with those impurities produced by that [wind],
likewise brings about all crops through rain.
Likewise, in the case of lotus ponds and so forth, there is the washing away of everything for everyone;
therefore, nothing such as "pure" or "impure" exists here at all. (8)
(36) If there were some purity, impurity would exist;
but since purity does not exist, impurity is not apprehended in any way whatsoever. // 9 //
Just as the concepts of "this shore" and "the other shore" are relative to one another, so too this conceptualization of the pure and the impure is merely a worldly construction. (10)
In the *Jñānasiddhi*, the tenth chapter is titled "The Discrimination Between the Conceptions of Pure and Impure."
(37) Chapter Eleven: An investigation is now conducted regarding even the approaching of those who should not be approached, as to how that is permitted and non-contradictory for yogins. (1)
For all embodied beings, there is indeed arising and destruction; and that occurs at all times within the three realms solely through the power of karma. (2)
The mother may become the father and the son, and the son may become the mother and the father;
the female servant may even become the wife, and the wife may likewise become the mother. (3)
Vajrasattva has taught that such forms as these, in their many varieties and great detail, exist within this beginningless cyclic existence. (4)
Such being the case, within this saṃsāra that has been evolving for a long time,
there is not a single sentient being who has not previously been one's mother or father.
Likewise, all those who have previously existed as daughters and so forth are present within the six realms of existence;
therefore, the supreme Jinas have declared that great compassion must be cultivated.
Therefore, those supreme protectors, Vajrasattva and the others, authorize daughters and so forth for yogins in the practice of the mind. (7)
Who indeed, having boarded the Vajrayāna, will cross to the further shore of this great ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with the waters of conceptual construction? (8)
All false cognitions, which are indeed mines of every defect, have been refuted in due order by means of arguments consistent with scripture. 9.
In the *Jñānasiddhi*, the eleventh chapter, titled "Devoid of the Distinguishable and the Indistinguishable," [is concluded].
(38) The Twelfth Chapter.
Now, for the sake of awakening the vajra-wisdom, reasoning is also set forth by means of examples taught in the Yoga Tantras, for the benefit of the supreme yogins. (1)
Just as entities such as the form-body (rūpakāya) do not possess the nature of reality, their exclusion has already been established; therefore, formlessness (arūpatva) remains. || 2 ||
Because it entails all faults, existence cannot be reality;
nor can non-existence be that reality, for it is the ultimate source of all suffering. (3)
Existence and non-existence are not reality; reality must be devoid of those two.
Therefore, it is not logical for it to be located in space; consequently, there would be no omniscient one at that time.
Pervasiveness, the state of possessing a vajra-body, and indeed immutability—therefore, omniscience is established as the perfection of right knowledge through reasoning. (5)
For that which possesses form has no omnipresence; therefore, there is no adamantine body (vajrakāya).
There is nothing unchangeable for it, nor will it ever become omniscient. (6)
Whoever knows everything only gradually does not attain awakening;
because the objects of knowledge are immeasurable, such a person is not accepted as omniscient. || 7 ||
Even in a thousand million eons, one would not be able to know even that which has been proclaimed as the object of knowledge in a single direction alone.
If destruction were to arise [only] after having been produced, then it would not be produced from that [cause];
rather, that knowledge is firmly established and serves solely to destroy delusion.
For that which undergoes coming and going, stability is not found;
because of its mobility, its destruction follows from remaining in a single location. (10)
(39) What dharma could there be that is beyond description, such that one would be capable of destroying it?
A Buddha may be born [in the world], but he is not born as a weapon, water, poison, or fire. 11.
Its self is established in all modes; it is immovable like the sky, undefiled, and changeless, existing in every way and at all times. (12)
But he who is not omniscient at all times would not be [omniscient];
therefore, it is traditionally taught that [the state of omniscience] must exist at all times. (13)
Thus this great gnosis abides within all embodied beings;
yet those fools, childish and shrouded by the veil of delusion, do not perceive it. (14)
When a clod of earth is thrown, it runs away, but the thrower does not run in that same way;
likewise, that which is to be pursued by the mind runs away, but the mind itself does not.
Whatever is spoken by the mind is indeed that very [mind] which is observed;
there arises no thought as to what this "mind" is like. (16)
In the *Jñānasiddhi*, the twelfth chapter is titled "The Establishment of Reality."

Chapter Thirteen This world is most deluded; for the sake of liberation, it exerts itself toward the determination of a self, even though—like one impelled by a rain-cloud—it is being cast down a precipice. (1)
Such behavior is observed even among many embodied beings;
having abandoned the vehicle of the Sugata, they resort to another path. (2)
If some person of that kind were to point out another path, even the questioner would not ask him [that by which reality is awakened]. (3)
If, due to the power of delusion, one does not perceive the guide who shows the path,
then no welfare is obtained by the traveler proceeding along that very path.
How can one who does not see the path himself lead another effectively?
If two were to go together, there would undoubtedly be suffering for both. (5)
Just as there might be an action for one born blind who has entered a forest, how could someone else lead such a second person into a village? (6)
Thus, being like those born blind and not seeing right knowledge, they are unable to reach that state themselves; how then could they cause another to reach it? (7)
Therefore, the supreme Jinas declare that disciples endowed with devotion must perform service to their gurus only after having examined them. (8)

One whose self is the Buddha within the Three Jewels, who is compassionate toward all sentient beings, who is steadfast and restrained in renunciation and other virtues, is the source of the great arising of all merit. || 9 ||
(41) One who has generated the mind of awakening, who is serene, virtuous, and wise; who is free from anger, possesses great enthusiasm, and has a profound certainty regarding the Dharma. || 10 ||
The gift of Dharma is always considered to be reasoned and free from conceptual appearance; he always possesses few desires and is fully endowed with the two accumulations. || 11 ||
This one is proclaimed as the Guru by all the Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders;
he alone is the teacher of all sentient beings and the leader of the world. (12)
And other renowned teachers, conceited in their false knowledge, deliver supreme instructions on the Dharma for the sake of greed and other such motives. (13)
Those fools are evil friends, established in the destruction of sentient beings;
they belong to the faction of Māra, are devoid of self-nature, and are destroyers. (14)
Those beings are to be avoided, and one should not attend upon them; one should not harbor resentment toward them, nor should they be considered more worthy of worship. || 15 ||
Just as dwelling together with the śrāvakas is not desired by the Tathāgatas, in the same way, dwelling together with those of such a kind is not considered superior. || 16 ||
Therefore, by means of the characteristics previously mentioned, one is indeed ordained as a teacher;
and now the characteristics of the disciple are likewise described, so that he may become such.
The thirteenth [chapter], the description of the characteristics of the Guru, in the Jñānasiddhi.
Chapter Fourteen Just as a certain well-trained helmsman, having boarded a ship, reaches the far shore of the great ocean, one cannot reach the other side otherwise. (1)
In the same way, devotion toward the Guru, the Three Jewels, and the spirit of enlightenment (bodhicitta), as well as compassion for the world—this is proclaimed to be the boat. (2)
The Guru is the helmsman, the wise one; Dharma is the manifest ship, taught by Vajrasattva for those who wish to go to the further shore of cyclic existence. (3)
Without a helmsman, a boat is not capable of reaching the further shore;
likewise, even if one is complete in all virtues, without a guru, one does not cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, for this very reason, all this must be performed by those of firm vows;
the yogi should always be devoted to worship, both external and internal.
Endowed with faith and wisdom, and moistened by compassion for all living beings, one should perform all rituals such as prostration at all times.
Free from anger and non-deceptive, adorned with virtues such as renunciation,
he is possessed of great vigor, possesses immense energy, and always carries out the command of his guru.

And having been thus instructed by the Buddhas themselves, one should perform service and so forth, providing food, meals, and the like according to one's ability and according to what is obtained. (8)
(43) Even when treated with contempt in this way, a disciple endowed with all virtues and one who examines through reasoning and scripture does not become dejected of his own accord. 9.
One who is not by nature a non-inquirer and who asks for the benefit of others is capable of being a disciple; thus it is demonstrated by the Buddhas. (10)
Just as a lump of clay is thrown here and there by children, so too is one who is under the control of others a fit vessel for discipleship. 11.
In the Jñānasiddhi, the fourteenth chapter, the examination of the characteristics of disciples.
Chapter Fifteen The correct reality, as it truly is, has been previously explained along with its logical reasoning. Now, that reality which abides in all tantras is being stated to you in brief. (1)
Just as the word *cora* in common worldly usage may convey the meaning of "food," some say it means "thief"; likewise, words function in the same way within the Tantra. (2)
By means of those very explanations of syllables—whether weak, middling, or superior—the Buddhas, who act for the benefit of sentient beings, speak of faith in the Dharma. (3)
Likewise, some person of middling faculties speaks only of reality;
some person of dull faculties speaks only of karma and nothing else. (4)

It is taught in the *Śrī-samājottara*: "Without beginning or end, peaceful, the indestructible of both existence and non-existence, all-pervading, and inseparable from emptiness and compassion—this is known as bodhicitta. (5)

"Without beginning or end" means the absence of arising and destruction. By this, its all-pervasiveness, immutability, and eternality are stated, because those things which are localized, material, subject to change, or limited by time are perishable.
Even though it is formless (*arūpitva*), if it were localized in space, it would necessarily be subject to destruction.

For example, the fragrance of musk and the like, although formless, would perish and undergo transformation due to its localization in space, in the absence of the musk or the substance perfumed by it.
It is "peaceful" because all afflictions are adventitious, and thus it is peaceful by nature.
Because it possesses the qualities previously mentioned, it is the inexhaustible state beyond existence and non-existence.
It is the pervasive, sovereign Lord, because it accomplishes all mundane and supramundane aims for everyone.

"Indivisible from emptiness and compassion" means that the mind which—through the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena—possesses the thorough knowledge of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, is indivisible and unified with emptiness by means of compassion.
What is called "compassion" is the thought: "I shall establish all sentient beings in this very King of Wisdom."
The correct intention is: "I shall surround [them] with all the requisites for happiness.

This is what is meant: the yogin who knows the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena always abides together with all the Tathāgatas in a state of mutual pervasion, performing the activities of a Buddha; for all sentient beings, his *bodhicitta*—which follows the immeasurable [qualities] of great compassion—is "Vajra. This is the meaning.
By this, it is demonstrated that cultivation should also be performed in this manner.
The statement "it is known as bodhicitta" intends this very point throughout all the Yoga Tantras.
For beginners and others, however, bodhicitta consists merely of the thought: "I shall establish all sentient beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Everything that was previously mentioned as the path, beginning with the prostrations, must all be performed; likewise, the verses and the members of the assembly [must be attended to].
Having instantly visualized oneself as one's own deity, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, the yogi established on the path should begin the recitation as before. (3)
At the conclusion, however, all the Buddhas together with their spiritual sons should grant me their favor; O you who are the refuge, may you, whose nature is compassion, show grace toward him.
Wandering in saṃsāra from beginningless time until now,
I am exhausted by constant sufferings, seeing no perfect knowledge.
I am prepared to act in such a way that the arising of knowledge may occur;
if one proceeds correctly, joined with this sequence,
the arising of knowledge will happen for him, but not for one who follows a false path.
The nineteenth chapter, the instruction on the method for those of middling faculties, in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
Chapter Twenty-Eight:

The great-armed [deities] are manifested through the colors, hand-symbols, maṇḍalas, and positions of the hands; they are also accessed by way of the three samādhis, the hand-symbols, and so forth. (1)
Because they are designated by various manifold names, all of them are traditionally considered to be "mṛdu" (soft).
Of these as well, I shall speak according to the proper method regarding their origin from reality.
Having established oneself upon the middling and superior paths according to the method,
one who mutters the deity's mantra must always perform that which is taught in the Tantra.
If one's mind is equanimous, for that person knowledge will arise;
otherwise, it cannot be attained even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Always endowed with contemplation, possessing great compassion, and being wise,
the yogi who is equipped with the previously mentioned characteristics shall obtain the supreme knowledge.
For the sake of the arising of correct knowledge, it has been taught by one who perceives no [other] activity that, in the two middle and final [stages], cultivation alone is primary. (6)
Without reality there is no Buddhahood, and without the path there is no reality;
therefore, it is only for those established on that path that the knowledge of the practice arises. (7)
For those whose minds are devoid of compassion and who have strayed from the path— being of a conceptual nature for the sake of gain and other such things— there shall be no spiritual awakening.
The twentieth chapter, the Exposition on the Faculties of Weak Capacity, in the *Jñānasiddhi*.
(69) This secret of such-and-such [a deity], concealed in all tantras, has been correctly taught by me for the sake of the attainment of wisdom by yogins. 1.
For those whose minds are intent on performing meditative cultivation in the forms of deities, yet in whom the supreme yoga of vajra-wisdom does not exist at all, [this is taught]. (2)
Even the sight of the book should not be granted by one who possesses knowledge;
through the rejection of vajra-wisdom, the deluded go to hell. (3)
Because that [offense] is a cause for hell, such a person would also go to Avīci;
since it results in such supreme misfortune, it must certainly be guarded against. (4)
"Otherwise, there would be a violation of the samaya," thus it was proclaimed by all the Buddhas, whose very nature is compassion, in numerous Yoga Tantras. (5)
This supreme adamantine gnosis, which has shaken off the web of conceptual construction, is the practice of Vajrasattva, established through the path and supported by reasoning. (6)
By whatever merit has been accumulated by me through composing this *Sādhanopāyikā*, may there be for all sentient beings the supreme state of Vajrasattva. (7)
The *Jñānasiddhi*, a manual of means for accomplishment originating from the illustrious Oḍḍiyāna, is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Indrabhūti. (70)
